summary: For 7–8 year olds learning to classify materials by observable properties, the core objective is a planned investigation (not casual sorting): choose ONE observable property, apply the SAME test to each material, record every result in a table, and only then classify from the recorded evidence — surfacing the pattern of which materials share the property, and seeing the same set regroup under a different property. The primary approach is a hands-on (or on-screen) investigation bench with live results logging; supporting approaches check the procedure with ordering/matching tasks and an annotated worked investigation.
misconceptions: Classifying by an untested surface feature (colour, size) or first impression rather than by a systematically tested property.
Applying the test inconsistently across materials, so the comparison and resulting classes are invalid.
Treating classification as a fixed property of the object, not realising the groups depend on the chosen criterion.
Skipping the record-then-classify discipline — grouping from memory or expectation instead of from the data table.
Confusing 'classify' (assign to groups by a rule) with merely 'describe' or with running a fair test for a purpose (a different enquiry type).

activities.title: Investigation bench: pick a property, test the same way, record, then classify
steps: Choose ONE observable property to test (e.g. 'is it magnetic?', hardness, or flexibility) from an offered set of age-appropriate, testable properties.
Commit to a single fixed test action and apply it identically to every material in turn (e.g. bring the same magnet to each material the same way).

Record each result as it happens in a table with materials down the side and the tested property across the top — e.g. steel paperclip yes, piece of copper pipe or wire no, wooden peg no, steel key yes. (Avoid using a coin as the 'copper' example: many 'copper' coins, such as UK 1p and 2p coins made since 1992, are copper-plated steel and are attracted to a magnet.)
Only after the table is complete, sort the materials into groups (e.g. 'magnetic' / 'not magnetic') and check that each group matches the recorded data.

Press a 'switch property' option to re-test the exact same materials under a second property (e.g. hardness) and watch them regroup — e.g. the steel key and a glass marble now share a group they did not before.
Name the shared-property group: say which materials clustered together and why.
Pair the screen work with a real tray of materials and a magnet to carry out the physical investigation alongside.
activities.insight: A classification is not a fixed fact about a material; it is the answer to the particular question you chose to test. Consistency of the test and grouping from recorded evidence (not first impressions) are what make it an investigation.

activities.title: Spot the flaw and order the steps (procedure checks)
steps: Put the stages of a classifying investigation into the correct order: plan the test → test each material the same way → record results in a table → classify from the results.
Given a short scenario, identify an inconsistent (unfair) test used within a classification — where one material was tested differently from the others.
Given a completed results table, pick the classification (grouping) that genuinely matches the recorded data.
Sort stated materials into groups by a named property.
activities.insight: Recognising the correct investigation sequence, consistent testing, and evidence-matching groups reinforces the structure of the skill — though recognising it is not the same as carrying it out.

activities.title: Walk through a completed investigation (annotated model)
steps: Examine a finished investigation showing the results table, the groups formed, and the shared-property pattern.
Reveal the reasoning behind each part: tap the table, the single test method, and each group to see why the materials were placed there.
Open a flap/panel that re-sorts the same materials under a second property and compare the two groupings.
Explain in your own words why the same materials ended up in different groups.
activities.insight: Seeing a fully worked, correctly structured investigation can make the plan→test→record→classify sequence and the criterion-dependence of groups explicit before or after doing one yourself.

checkQuestion: Put out five materials (steel paperclip, aluminium foil, copper coin, plastic counter, wooden bead) and a magnet. Say: 'Plan and carry out a test to find which are magnetic. Test each the same way, record what you find in a chart, then sort them into groups from your results.' Watch them plan, test and record.
checkAnswer: Brings the magnet to each material the same way, records a yes/no for each in a chart, and sorts into magnetic / non-magnetic groups strictly from the recorded results — finding that only the steel paperclip is attracted, and that the other metals (aluminium, copper) are NOT.
